subject: covariates for density that cannot be measured across the state space

messages.author: 55d961293add928a
messages.subject: covariates for density that cannot be measured across the state space
parts:
Hi,

I am using a single-session secr model to investigate the density of a leopard population surveyed with camera traps. As part of the analysis, I am interested in whether the relative abundance of competitors (lions and hyenas) and prey affects density. I can calculate these variables at the stations based on photographic captures, but I cannot measure these variables across the state space and so I cannot include them in the model as covariates for density. Is there a way around this issue?

In this particular component of the analysis, I care more about whether these factors affect density than I do about the density itself. I'm just spit-balling here but could I randomly assign observed values at the camera stations to pixels in the state space in order to fit a model? 

Any insights would be greatly appreciated.

Matt

messages.subject: RE: covariates for density that cannot be measured across the state space
parts:
Matt,

We have exactly the same problem. We need to include abundance of prey (guanacos) for pumas in Patagonia as a covariate. We have estimates of guanacos from cameras but do not have measures across the state space.  Certainly many studies would have this issue for either competitors or prey. Please keep me informed of your final solution.   

 

Thanks.

 

Lyn

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: AW: covariates for density that cannot be measured across the state space
parts:
Hi all,

 

When you have a covariate that is missing you can estimate the missing values. That can be done with different levels of sophistication. Cheapest is to replace the missings with covariate average. This has various disadvantages but may be acceptable if the proportion of sites in the entire landscape with missings is low. More sophisticated methods specify explicit models for the covariate and estimate the missings that way. One of the cheapest there might be some sort of spatial interpolation such as kriging.

 

Ideally, the uncertainty in the estimated covariate values is propagated into the estimands from the SCR model, and this can only/easiest be done in a Bayesian mode of inference. But perhaps you are happy with a first stab at the problem with ignoring that uncertainty and treating the estimated prey density as if they were measured data.

 

A lot more could be said here, but the basic idea is that you have to somehow estimate the missing covariates if you want to use them in the model for the predator.

 

Best regards  -- Marc

messages.author: 2c49652a5796ed9c
messages.subject: Re: covariates for density that cannot be measured across the state space
parts: Another possible way to interpolate between the traps would be to fit an unmarked SCR model (I'm assuming prey are not individually identifiable) and use the realized density surface as a density covariate for the focal species. This could be done in a manner that incorporates the uncertainty in the "interpolation" into the density beta for the focal species. Unmarked SCR has pretty steep data requirements, but informative priors for sigma could be used, and if the goal is not so much the absolute density of the prey species, but something that correlates with it, this might be a good metric to use. However, this is much more complicated than interpolation and not clearly any better. Just throwing this idea out there.
